name: Manx

allophone_rules.notes: Goidelic slender/broad marking: a written vowel letter (i/e) before a word-final n marks the n as palatalised ('slender'). WikiPron/Wiktionary gold shows the marker surfacing as an epenthetic schwa before the palatalised n in the large majority of -in/-ein/-ain finals -- Mannin [manənʲ], aalin [ɛːlinʲ] (with i realised, not schwa, but still non-null), aynin [unənʲ], benrein [benreːnʲ], blein [bleːnʲ], cuishlin [kuʃlʲənʲ], dourin [daurənʲ], glashtin [ɡlaʃtʲənʲ], marin [mɛːrʲənʲ], orrin [orənʲ], shiaghtin [ʃaxtʲənʲ] (WikiPron glv_latn_broad). A minority of forms, notably dowin [daunʲ] and ain [ain] (no palatalisation at all), show no schwa (Broderick 1984-86, A Handbook of Late Spoken Manx, vol.3; Thomson 1992, 'The Manx Language', in MacAulay (ed.) The Celtic Languages, ch.3); this variation is documented, not encoded, since the schwa-bearing form dominates the cited transcriptions. Uses mutates_neighbor: the rule keeps its own slot as [ə] while palatalising the FOLLOWING slot (the final n) atomically -- see docs/allophony.md.

Goidelic slender/broad marking, onset case: a written i/e between an onset consonant and a following vowel marks the consonant as palatalised ('slender') and does not itself surface -- Manx giare [ɡʲɛːr], giat [ɡʲat] (Broderick 1984-86; Thomson 1992, ch.3). mutates_neighbor palatalises the PRECEDING slot atomically as the vowel deletes.

ancestors.notes: English adstrate: heavy influence, English-based orthography

notes: Manx (Gaelg). Isle of Man. Last native speaker (Ned Maddrell) died 1974. Revival since 1970s; ~1,800 speakers (est. 2020). English/Welsh-based orthography descending from Bishop John Phillips' Book of Common Prayer tradition (unlike Irish/Scots Gaelic script). Simplified mutation system vs. Irish/Scots Gaelic. Characteristic digraphs/trigraphs: <gh> word-final/preconsonantal realises [x] (Broderick 1984-86 vol.3; only rarely [ɣ] intervocalically); <çh> /tʃ/ contrasts with <ch> /x/; <sh> /ʃ/; <aa> is predominantly [ɛː] (Broderick), not the older [eː]; word-final <ey> reduces to unstressed [ə] (long [əː] when it is the stressed nucleus, e.g. monosyllables); <nn>/<mm>/<rr> are English-style doubled-consonant spellings marking a preceding short vowel, not gemination, and surface as a single (sometimes palatalised) consonant; <ng> is the velar nasal [ŋ]. Preocclusion of final nasals/liquids (<nn>→[dn], <mm>→[bm]) described for fuller Late Spoken Manx phonetic transcriptions (Broderick 1984-86; Jackson 1955) is NOT attested in the WikiPron/Wiktionary broad-transcription gold used here, which instead shows plain (non-preoccluded) [n]/[m] throughout — the gold reflects a lenited, revival-adjacent register rather than Broderick's narrow phonetic fieldwork transcriptions; preocclusion is therefore documented here rather than encoded, pending a gold source that attests it. Gaelic slender/broad (caol/leathan) consonant marking survives vestigially: an adjacent <i>/<e> can signal a palatalised neighbouring consonant without itself surfacing as a vowel (e.g. giare [ɡʲɛːr], dowin [daunʲ]) — modelled by the GV_SLENDER_FINAL_N / GV_SLENDER_ONSET_CONSONANT allophone_rules, using the generic mutates_neighbor mechanism (a rule deletes its own vowel slot while palatalising an adjacent consonant slot atomically; see docs/allophony.md, section 'Marker graphemes'). ⟨eu⟩ is kept as its own grapheme key despite its IPA reading as the concatenation of ⟨e⟩+⟨u⟩'s primary values: it spells a single diphthongal nucleus (WikiPron gold 'eu' [eu], 'feue' [feu]), the same unit-nucleus justification as ⟨ai⟩/⟨aaj⟩ elsewhere in the schema, not an enumerated pair. The English-derived orthography carries digraphs whose English values are false friends: ⟨th⟩ is /t/, not a dental fricative — Manx has no /θ ð/ at all (Lewin 2020: thalloo/thallooin /taˈluːnʲ/, thie /tai/) — and ⟨lh⟩ is the palatalised lateral /lʲ/ rather than /l/+/h/ (lhean /lʲeːn/, lhiabbee /lʲabi/, lhune /lʲuːn/, lhiaght /lʲaxt/). ⟨y⟩ is /j/ as an onset but a vowel letter elsewhere, reading [ə] or [i] (Jamys /dʒeːməs/, fys /fis/); it is split positionally. The vowel digraphs and trigraphs follow Lewin's orthography-to-phone tables (2020: 69-71): ⟨oa⟩ /oː/ (noa /noː/), ⟨ae⟩ /ɛː/ (aeg /ɛːɡ/), ⟨ea⟩ /eː/ with /ɛː/ beside it (rea /reː/, gearey /ɡɛːrʲə/), ⟨eea⟩ /iə/ (geearree, jeeaghyn), ⟨eay⟩ /əː/ (bleayst /bləːst/), ⟨aue⟩ /ɛːu/ (laue, raaue, snaue), ⟨aih aie aigh aaie⟩ /ɛːi/ (graih /ɡrɛːi/, traie /trɛːi/, aigh /ɛːi/, faaie /fɛːi/), ⟨aiy⟩ /eː/ (faiyr /feːr/), ⟨ay⟩ /e/ or /eː/ (aym /em/, kay /kʲeː/), ⟨oie⟩ /əi/ or /iː/ (roie), and ⟨uy⟩ /əː/ (Gaelic aoi gives Manx /əː/, Lewin 2020 §3.4.2; nuy < naoi). ⟨eih⟩ is given as /əː/ before /əi/: both are attested (seihll /səːl/, leih /ləi/, Lewin 2020: 69), and the ordering is a distributional choice made on the gold, not a ranking Lewin states. Doubled consonant letters are English-style vowel-length markers rather than geminates, so collapse_geminates is on; the ⟨i⟩ that flanks them is the palatalisation marker (ooilley /ulʲə/, bainney /banʲə/, cuirrey /kurʲə/, troiddey /trodʲə/, Lewin 2020: 72). The apostrophe marks elision and is silent. NOT a Goidelic template: the gv grapheme table was checked key-by-key against ga and gd, which share the same cel-x-goidelic parent. Of the 25 keys gv shares with ga, one carries the same value; of the 25 it shares with gd, six do, and those six are ⟨e f h m ng r⟩. The Manx table is its own. Refs: Lewin (2020), Thomson (1992), Broderick (1984-86), Jackson (1955).
